title: Three nights, three boons
theme: Yama greets the boy with honour and offers a boon for each night he waited without food.

words.role: with trīn varān: one for each [night]

sandhi.type: visarga before voiced sounds; t before a vowel
sandhi.rule: īḥ → īr before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः); yat → yad before a vowel, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
A final n after a short vowel is doubled before a vowel, P. 8.3.32 (ङमो ह्रस्वादचि ङमुण्नित्यम्).
aḥ → as before t, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः); te + astu → te ’stu, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति).

sandhi_exceptions.note: The base prints me anaśnan unjoined (Śaṅkara’s mūla and gloss «गृहे मे मम अनश्नन्»); the vishvAsa mūla and Raṅgarāmānuja write me ’naśnan with the a elided (corrections.json).

morphology.note: s-aorist of vas, ‘dwell’, 2nd person: ‘you have stayed’. GRETIL’s avatsīḥ with a short a is a slip (corrections.json).
Gerundive of the denominative namasya-, ‘to pay homage’: ‘one to whom homage is due’.
Imperative middle of vṛ, ‘choose’ (class 9): ‘choose for yourself’.

translation.literal: Since you have stayed three nights in my house without eating, O brāhmaṇa, a guest worthy of reverence — reverence be to you, O brāhmaṇa; may there be well-being for me! Therefore choose three boons, [one] for each.
translation.readable: ‘Brāhmaṇa, you are a guest who deserves honour, and you have stayed three nights in my house without food. Reverence to you! Let it be well with me. So choose three boons, one for each night.’

anvaya: ब्रह्मन्, नमस्यः अतिथिः [त्वम्] यत् मे गृहे तिस्रः रात्रीः अनश्नन् अवात्सीः, [तस्मात्] ब्रह्मन् ते नमः अस्तु, मे स्वस्ति अस्तु । तस्मात् [एकैकां रात्रिम्] प्रति त्रीन् वरान् वृणीष्व ॥
syntax: A causal clause (‘since you stayed…’), two wishes in the imperative (‘reverence be to you’, ‘well-being be to me’) and the command ‘choose three boons’. Prati, ‘for each’, links the three boons to the three nights.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: one for each night spent fasting — «अनशनेनोषितामेकैकां रात्रिं प्रति त्रीन् वरान् वृणीष्व». Raṅgarāmānuja says the same and adds that Yama offers them for his own sake, though the boy wants nothing: «तव लिप्साभावेऽपि मदनुग्रहार्थम्».
A later Dvaita commentator on Madhva (Vedeśatīrtha) asks whether the words could be the wife’s, and concludes from the context that they are Yama’s.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Triṣṭubh, 22 + 20 syllables as written: the first line counts the unjoined hiatus me anaśnan (21 if elided); the second has two short pādas of ten as printed.

beginner: Death comes home and finds the boy who has waited three nights at his door without food. He greets him with real respect: you are a guest worthy of honour; reverence to you. Then he adds a wish for himself: may it go well with me. He knows he has done wrong by a guest, and that this matters. To set things right he offers three boons, one for each night of fasting. Here the story turns. A boy given away in anger to Death is now offered anything he wishes by Death himself. What will he ask for? The next verses tell us, and the third request will become the subject of the whole Upaniṣad.
analogy: Like a host who returns late to find a guest has waited for days, apologises sincerely, and says: name three things I can do for you.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Yama greets the boy with reverence, wishes well-being for himself, and offers three boons, one for each night the boy stayed without food.

commentary.q: Why does Yama wish well for himself?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: to be free of the fault of a guest’s fasting in his house; even if all would be well by the boy’s favour, Yama offers more to win him fully: «त्वदधिकसम्प्रसादनार्थम्» … «अनशनेनोषितामेकैकां रात्रिं प्रति त्रीन् वरान् वृणीष्व».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: That the boons are for Yama’s sake, not the boy’s: «तव लिप्साभावेऽपि मदनुग्रहार्थम् अनशनरात्रिसमसंख्याकान् त्रीन् वरान् वृणीष्व इति भावः».

commentary.q: How does Madhva read the three boons?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s verse on this passage: «इत्युक्तस्स यमस्तं तु सम्पूज्यादाद् वरत्रयम्» — so addressed, Yama honoured him and gave three boons. The verse he cites next (from what he calls the Gatisāra) names them in advance: the father’s goodwill, Hari in the Nāciketa fire, and Viṣṇu present in the released — «सौमनस्यं पितुश्चैव नाचिकेताग्निगं हरिम्» … «मुक्ते स्थितञ्च तं विष्णुमिति प्रादात् वरत्रयम्» (reported as cited by Madhva).

advaita.text: Three boons, one for each night of fasting: «अनशनेनोषितामेकैकां रात्रिं प्रति त्रीन् वरान् वृणीष्व».

visistadvaita.text: Yama offers the boons for his own good, the boy having no desire: «तव लिप्साभावेऽपि मदनुग्रहार्थम्».

dvaita.text: Yama honours the boy and grants three boons («इत्युक्तस्स यमस्तं तु सम्पूज्यादाद् वरत्रयम्»), which a verse Madhva cites reads as the father’s goodwill, Hari in the Nāciketa fire and Viṣṇu in the released: «सौमनस्यं पितुश्चैव नाचिकेताग्निगं हरिम्».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja explain why there are three boons; Madhva’s cited verse already reads the second and third as knowledge of Viṣṇu, not of a fire-rite and a question about the dead.

contemporary.text: A powerful figure who has wronged someone apologises, names the wrong, and offers real redress rather than excuses. This is a modern reflection, not the text’s claim.

reflect.beginner: When you have wronged someone, how do you try to make it right?
reflect.deeper: Why does Yama ask for well-being for himself in the same breath as honouring the boy?
reflect.practice: Make a concrete amends today for one small wrong you have done.

flags.note: The base prints me anaśnan unjoined; GRETIL reads avatsīḥ with a short a (a slip) (corrections.json).
